job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Superintelligence Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Superintelligence Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Superintelligence Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COVERED AI SYSTEM.—The term "covered AI system" means—
  (A) an artificial intelligence model trained using a quantity of computing power greater than 10^26 integer or floating-point operations in a single training run; or
  (B) any artificial intelligence system that the Secretary determines is capable of substantially exceeding human performance across most cognitive tasks.
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED FACILITY.—The term "covered facility" means a data center containing more than 50,000 advanced AI chips.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to train, develop, or deploy a covered AI system.
(b) EXISTING SYSTEMS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to a covered AI system whose training began before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) SAFETY EVALUATION.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of safety evaluation.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered facility shall register the facility with the Department of Commerce.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the Department of Commerce a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the computing workloads run at the facility.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that covered AI systems can be developed safely.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Issues in S. 2817 (Superintelligence Prohibition Act, as amended October 6, 2026)

I reviewed only the text you provided. I can't see the introduced version, so I can't tell what the manager's amendment changed. Some items below could cut either way: broad terms may overreach, and narrow ones may leave gaps. Verify the final list against the official text and CRS or Senate Legislative Counsel before publication.

**Coverage thresholds and definitions**

1. **§2(1)(A), "single training run":** Measuring compute per run lets developers split training across multiple runs or count only the final stage. Post-threshold fine-tuning, continued pretraining, and reinforcement learning may also fall outside the definition. The bill also doesn't say how FLOPs are counted (estimated or measured, and which operations).
2. **§2(1)(A), fixed threshold:** The 10^26 figure has no mechanism for updating it. Algorithmic efficiency could produce comparable capabilities below the line.
3. **§2(1)(A) vs. §3(a), "model" vs. "system":** Subsection (A) defines a covered "model," but §3 prohibits a "covered AI system." It's unclear whether an agent, product, or wrapper built on a covered model is itself covered.
4. **§2(1)(B), undefined "Secretary":** The bill doesn't say which Secretary makes the determination. It also sets no procedure, criteria, notice, timeline, or judicial review for designations.
5. **§2(1)(B), undefined capability terms:** "Substantially exceeding," "most cognitive tasks," and "human performance" have no stated benchmark, baseline population, or method. Combined with criminal penalties, this invites vagueness challenges.
6. **§2(1)(B), no effective date for designations:** The bill doesn't say whether a designation applies to systems already in development or deployed, or how a company learns it is covered before it violates §3.
7. **§2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition covers citizens and corporations organized under state law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, federally chartered entities, permanent residents, and foreign-organized subsidiaries of U.S. companies. A U.S. company could route training through a foreign-organized affiliate.
8. **§2(3), "covered facility":** "Data center," "advanced AI chips," and "containing" are all undefined. Leased, cloud-based, or geographically distributed capacity may fall outside the definition.
9. **§2(3) vs. §3, registry gap:** The 50,000-chip threshold appears only in the registry provision. The prohibition doesn't reference it, so training below that threshold, or at unregistered sites, isn't constrained by the registry.
10. **Missing definitions:** The bill doesn't define "person" (it relies on the default in 1 U.S.C. §1, which generally doesn't reach government entities), "operator," "train," "develop," "deploy," "State" (whether DC and territories count), or "safety evaluation."

**Prohibition scope and exemptions**

11. **§3(a), "train, develop, or deploy":** These terms are undefined and overlap. It's unclear whether releasing open weights, offering API access, fine-tuning a covered model, or doing research on one counts.
12. **§3(a), enabling conduct not addressed:** The prohibition doesn't reach providing compute, chips, cloud capacity, model weights, or financing for covered training. It's also unclear whether commissioning a third party (possibly abroad) to train a covered system counts as "training" by the commissioning U.S. person.
13. **§3(a), reach abroad:** "Any U.S. person anywhere" depends on the narrow §2(2) definition (see item 7). Foreign persons abroad using U.S. cloud services or U.S.-origin chips aren't clearly covered. The bill also doesn't address service of process or venue for foreign defendants.
14. **§3(b), grandfathering:** The exemption is keyed to when training "began," not when it finished. "Began" is undefined, and the exemption as written covers development and deployment of those systems indefinitely, not only the training run.
15. **§3(b) and §8, pre-effective window:** Subsection (b) uses the enactment date, but the prohibition doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Training started in that gap is grandfathered, which creates an incentive to start runs before the prohibition applies.
16. **§3(c), safety evaluation exemption:** "Purpose of safety evaluation" is undefined and turns on intent, which is hard to verify. The bill doesn't require notice, registration, or scope limits. It's also unclear whether the exemption covers training a new covered system or only evaluating a trained one, and whether it allows customer-facing deployment for testing.
17. **§3 and government actors:** Because "person" generally doesn't reach government entities, federal agencies and national labs may fall outside the prohibition. The bill doesn't say so either way.

**Registry and reporting (§4)**

18. **§4(a), registration mechanics:** The bill sets no registration deadline, no content requirements, and no public listing. "Operator" doesn't distinguish between the facility owner and a tenant running workloads.
19. **§4(b), report content:** "Describing the computing workloads" doesn't require identifying training runs, FLOP totals, or specific models. The registry therefore can't verify compliance with §3.
20. **§4, no enforcement:** Failure to register or file isn't a violation of §3, so §5 doesn't reach it. The bill also states no consequence for a false certification beyond general law.
21. **§4, no audit or verification authority and no confidentiality protection:** The bill grants no inspection rights and doesn't protect proprietary information from disclosure. Both could deter accurate reporting.
22. **§4(b), first report date:** No start date is set for the first quarterly report.

**Penalties and enforcement (§5)**

23. **§5, no enforcing agency:** The bill doesn't say whether DOJ, Commerce, or a private party brings civil actions. It also gives no authority for injunctions, cease-and-desist orders, or seizure of chips, weights, or facilities.
24. **§5(a), unit of violation:** "For each day on which the violation occurs" doesn't say whether a violation is counted per model, per run, per chip, per facility, or per day. A single long run could yield one day's penalty, and $1 million per day may be small relative to training costs.
25. **§5(a) vs. §8, date conflict:** The civil penalty applies to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. It's unclear whether conduct in that gap is penalized.
26. **§5(b), "willfully":** The standard is undefined. A defendant could argue it didn't know a run crossed the threshold or that a Secretary designation applied. The bill also says nothing about attempt, conspiracy, or officer liability.
27. **§5, penalties only for §3:** No penalties attach to §4 noncompliance, including false certifications or failure to report.
28. **§5(a), limitations period:** The bill sets none. The default federal limitations period for civil penalties (28 U.S.C. §2462, generally five years) would likely apply; staff should confirm.

**International agreement (§6)**

29. **§6, "shall seek to negotiate":** This is hortatory, with no reporting deadline, no consequence for failure, and no stated effect on §3 if an agreement is reached or fails. "Equivalent" is also undefined.

**Duration and sunset (§7)**

30. **§7(a), joint resolution:** A joint resolution is generally presented to the President for signature or veto, and the bill doesn't say otherwise. The required majority, the process, and the meaning of "finds" are unspecified.
31. **§7(a), "can be developed safely":** "Safely" is undefined. The NASEM report has no deadline or required content, and nothing requires Congress to act on it.
32. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), conflicting duration:** Subsection (a) makes the prohibition indefinite, but subsection (b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. If (b) controls, (a) does little; if (a) controls, (b) is inconsistent with it.
33. **§7(b), no savings clause:** The bill doesn't say what happens to pending enforcement actions, accrued penalties, or registry obligations when the Act ends.
34. **§7(a), mismatch with §2:** The finding concerns "covered AI systems," but it's unclear whether that means the §2 definition, which has two prongs and a Secretary designation, or some other category.

**General implementation and challenge exposure**

35. **No severability clause:** If a key provision falls (for example, the §2(1)(B) designation power or the extraterritorial reach), the status of the rest of the Act is uncertain.
36. **No rulemaking authority:** Commerce has registry duties but no authority to issue regulations defining terms, FLOP measurement methods, or registry forms. Implementation depends on undefined terms.
37. **No funding or implementation timeline:** The bill provides no appropriations for the registry or enforcement, and no schedule for standing up either.
38. **Constitutional exposure:** Vagueness challenges are likely given the criminal penalties and undefined terms. Nondelegation challenges are possible given the open-ended §2(1)(B) determination. The bill's restrictions on "develop" could also draw First Amendment challenges if they reach publication of research or code, and the bill doesn't address that. Extraterritorial application is another likely point of challenge.
39. **No judicial review provision:** The bill doesn't specify forum or standard of review for §2(1)(B) determinations. The Administrative Procedure Act may fill the gap, but that would need to be confirmed.
40. **No preemption or savings clause:** The bill doesn't say whether states may adopt stricter or parallel rules, which invites litigation over conflicts.
41. **No whistleblower protection:** Employees who report violations get no statutory protection, which weakens detection under a regime that depends on self-reporting.

**Suggested next steps before Thursday**

- Pull the introduced text and the manager's amendment's comparison to see what changed.
- Confirm the Secretary, enforcing agency, and §2462 points with CRS or Senate Legislative Counsel.
- Prioritize items 1, 7, 12, 14, 23, 24, 30, and 32 for committee coverage, since they most directly affect whether covered activity can continue and how the Act would be enforced.
